title: Replicating Covert CoT Sandbagging Against Various Monitor Strengths

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling and critical: scalable oversight depends on monitors catching deceptive reasoning. Empirically measuring the monitor-capability gap is foundational for evaluating whether CoT monitoring works as a safety mechanism.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires prompted sandbagging setup, deploying monitors of multiple sizes (7B to 70B), and measuring detection rates. Running 70B models for both target and monitor needs significant compute and ML experience.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple monitor sizes times two benchmarks (HumanEval, MMLU) is a sustained experimental matrix. The study is well-defined but covers a substantial parameter space for 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: The core question of whether CoT monitoring catches sandbagging is partially addressed by multiple 2025 papers showing bypass rates of 16-36% and monitor AUROCs of 0.91. However, a systematic sweep of monitor sizes (7B to 70B) against sandbagging specifically has not been published, leaving room for a focused replication contribution.

evidence: Korbak et al. (2025) 'Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety' (arXiv:2507.11473) establishes that CoT monitoring is fragile and can collapse under optimization pressure.
arXiv:2508.00943 'LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring' shows frontier and smaller models achieving 16-36% bypass rates against CoT monitors.
A pragmatic measurement paper (arXiv:2510.23966) introduces legibility and coverage metrics for CoT monitorability.
MALT dataset (METR 2025) includes sandbagging detection with monitors reaching 0.91 AUROC.
However, systematic study of monitor-capability gap across a range of monitor sizes (7B to 70B) has not been comprehensively published.
